blocks.text: Carbohydrates are naturally occurring organic compounds, including sugars, starch and cellulose and substances in bacterial cell walls and insect exoskeletons. They are major sources of energy in our diet. Chemically they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds derived from them; they are also called 'hydrates of carbon'.

Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates, the simple sugars such as glucose and fructose; they cannot be hydrolysed into simpler sugars. Their general formula is Cn(H2O)n, where n is from three to seven: a triose has three carbon atoms, a tetrose four, a pentose five and a hexose six. They are also classified by their functional group: an aldose has an aldehyde group and a ketose a ketone group. Glucose is an aldose and fructose a ketose.

Monosaccharides exist as open chains or as rings; sugars with five carbons (pentoses) or six carbons (hexoses) are more stable, and more abundant, as rings. In their solid form they exist as rings, and in solution most of their molecules also exist as rings, in equilibrium with a small amount of the linear structure. Fructose forms a five-membered ring (furanose) and glucose a six-membered ring (pyranose). The open-chain and ring forms interconvert: the OH on C5 of glucose adds to the C=O of C1, closing the ring.

blocks.text: The many hydroxyl groups of sugar molecules give extensive hydrogen bonding between their molecules, so pure monosaccharides are solids. In solution they form extensive hydrogen bonds with water, which makes them very soluble. Monosaccharides are an excellent source of instant energy: glucose is called blood sugar because it is present in human blood, while fructose is abundant in fruits and honey. (The thickness of honey comes from the strong hydrogen bonding of its fructose and glucose.)

Disaccharides consist of two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic linkage, generally with the formula C12H22O11; common ones are sucrose, lactose and maltose. They form by a condensation reaction: a hydroxyl group of one monosaccharide combines with the hydrogen of a hydroxyl group of another, releasing a molecule of water. The resulting C-O-C bond is the glycosidic bond. Sucrose, table sugar, is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose.

blocks.alt: Glucose (six-membered ring) and fructose (five-membered ring) drawn as Haworth rings; the H of the OH on glucose C1 and the HO on fructose C2 are boxed. An arrow leads to sucrose, in which C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose are joined through one oxygen atom, labelled 'glycosidic linkage in sucrose', + H2O.

blocks.text: Polysaccharides are large molecules made of a large number of monosaccharide units joined together, with high molecular masses and the general formula (C6H10O5)n. They give monosaccharides on hydrolysis. Common examples are starch, glycogen, cellulose and pectin.

items: Starch is the main energy store of plants and consists of glucose units. It has two components: amylose, with long unbranched chains, and amylopectin, a compact, highly branched structure. Potato, sugar beet, rice and grains contain large amounts of starch.

Cellulose is the main structural material of plant cell walls. It consists of glucose units (up to about 2500) in long unbranched chains; the chains form strong hydrogen bonds with each other, making cellulose rigid and insoluble in water. In human food it is fibre, which improves gut health.
Glycogen (animal starch) is a glucose polymer stored in the liver and muscles of animals. Its structure is like amylopectin but more highly branched.

blocks.alt: a) Amylose: three glucose rings joined C1-O-C4, each link labelled alpha-link (C1-C4), 1,4 glycosidic linkage. b) Amylopectin: two rows of glucose rings joined C1-O-C4, and a branch where C1 of an upper ring is joined through O to the CH2 (C6) of a lower ring, the 1,6 glycosidic linkage. c) Cellulose: three glucose rings with the carbons written as C, joined through O by beta links.
